¶

End-to-end Machine Learning Project¶

Below is the recipe that we are going to use to solve this problem:

  1. Frame the problem The objective of this change is to learn, but, we will act as if we are working for a major bank in the country.

    • Business Objective: be able to identify frauds as soon as possible in order to product our customers, what will enhance trust in our services and in turn improve customer satisfaction.
    • How will the solution be used? - We will evaluate transaction and block all suspected transaction, but we will also learn what a fraud looks like so that we can drive our outbound campaigns to improve customer literacy.
    • Current Solution? - As of now, we rely on complains coming from customer on our call center.
    • How we frame the problem? - This is a supervised regression task
    • Performance Measure? - We are going to be using A receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC Curve)

  2. Get the data

    • The data for this project was prepered by our data engineering team based on our data requirements for training the model (https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/playground-series-s6e11/data)
    • [Get the data]

  3. Explore the data to gain insight

    • [EDA]

  4. Prepare the data for ML algorithms

    • [Data Prep and Feature Engineering]

  5. Explore different ML models

    • [ML Modeling]

  6. Fine-tune and combine models

    • [Finetuning]

  7. Evaluate the solution

    • [Solution]

# Numeric features: compare distributions for fraud and non-fraud transactions.
ncols = 3
nrows = int(np.ceil(len(numeric_features) / ncols))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(16, 4 * nrows))

for ax, feature in zip(axes, numeric_features):

    sns.boxplot(data=train, x="is_fraud", y=feature, showfliers=False, ax=ax)

for ax in axes[len(numeric_features):]:
    ax.remove()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Explanation¶

From the box-plot above, these are the things that come into mind:

Feature Explanation
CVV_RETRY_COUNT For non-fraud, the box and whiskers all sit at 0, so almost nobody retries the CVV. For fraud, the median is 0 but Q3 is 1 and the whisker reaches 2, so at least 25% of fraud cases have a CVV retry. Any retry is a big red flag.
MERCHANT_RISK_SCORE The fraud median is about 46 versus about 34 for non-fraud, and the fraud box (≈38–55) sits mostly above the non-fraud box (≈26–42). Fraud happens at riskier merchants.
VELOCITY_SCORE The fraud median is about 27 versus about 18, and the whole fraud box is shifted up. Fraud comes with rapid, bursty activity.
TXN_COUNT_LAST_24H The fraud median is 4 versus 3, and the box is 3–5 versus 2–4. Fraudulent cards are used more often within a day.
CUSTOMER_AGE The fraud median is about 62 versus about 52, and the box is ≈48–73 versus ≈38–66. Older customers are targeted more.

The rest of the graph have weak signals, showing higher overlaps

Explanation¶

Reference point, the fraud rate in our dataset is 1.7%, so, when reading the bars we should see how far it sits above or below the baseline.

Feature What we see vs. baselibe
ip_country_mismatch True ~ 16.5%, False ~ 1.5% ~ 10x higher
is_ai_generated_scam_attempt True ≈ 15%, False ≈ 1.6% ~9× higher
billing_shipping_mismatch True ≈ 13%, False ≈ 1.5% ~8× higher
is_foreign_transaction True ≈ 12.6%, False ≈ 1.5% ~8× higher
auth_method No Authentication ≈ 6.5%, then 3D Secure ≈ 1.5%, OTP ≈ 1.4%, PIN ≈ 0.9%, Biometric ≈ 0.5% No auth is ~4× baseline. the stronger the authentication, the less fraud.
merchant_category Gift Cards ≈ 7.2%, Crypto Exchange ≈ 6.6%, Gaming ≈ 5.5%, Electronics ≈ 3.1%, then a slide to ≈1. The top three are categories where stolen money is easy to cash out or resell.
used_vpn True ≈ 6.4%, False ≈ 1.5% ~4× higher
is_new_merchant True ≈ 4.6%, False ≈ 1.2% ~4× higher.
Fraudsters tend to use the card somewhere the cardholder hasn't shopped before.

Correlation Analysis¶

Correlation is a statical method commonly used to measure the relationship between two variables, which establishes:

  1. Strength of the relationship (how far from |x| where -1<= x <=1)
  2. Direction of the relationship (positive or negative)
Correlation Coefficient Interpretation (Colton, 1974)
0 - 0.25 Little or no relationship
0.26 - 0.5 Fair degree of relationship
0.51 - 0.75 Moderate to good relationship
0.76 - 1 Very good to excellent relationship

Types of correlation¶

  • Pearson Correlation - Measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continues variables that come from a population, meaning that the variables have a normal distribution.
  • Spearman's rank correlation - Measures relationship between two variables using their ranked values (non-parametric test), the data is ordinal and not normally distributed.
  • Kendall's correlation - used to assess the ordinal association between two variables, it compares the number of concordant and discordant pairs. more robust than spearman when data has many tied ranks or small sample sizes.
  • Point biserial correlation - Measures the relationship between one continous variable and one binary (dichotomous) variable. example: you want to measure if gender (M=0, F=1) is related to math test scores.

def cyclic(period):
    def transform(X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        return np.hstack([np.sin(2 * np.pi * X / period), np.cos(2 * np.pi * X / period)])

    def names(_, input_features):
        return [f"{f}_sin" for f in input_features] + [f"{f}_cos" for f in input_features]

    return FunctionTransformer(transform, feature_names_out=names)


preprocess = ColumnTransformer(
    [
        ("scaled", StandardScaler(), scaled_cols),
        ("skewed", make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one"),StandardScaler()), skewed_cols),
        ("hour", cyclic(24), ["time_of_day_hour"]),
        ("day", cyclic(7), ["day_of_week"]),
        ("bool", FunctionTransformer(lambda X: X.astype(int), feature_names_out="one-to-one"), bool_cols),
        ("auth", StandardScaler(), ["auth_method"]),
        ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), nominal_cols),
    ],
    remainder="drop",
    verbose_feature_names_out=False,
).set_output(transform="pandas")

ML Modeling — Base classification models¶

We reuse the preprocess ColumnTransformer from above for every model, so the only thing that changes between experiments is the classifier.

We focus on PR-AUC (average precision) next to ROC-AUC: with only 1.7% fraud, ROC-AUC and accuracy look good even for weak models.

In [24]:
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_validate, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, confusion_matrix, classification_report, precision_recall_curve

# Applying the same transformations from "Creating additional features" to the test set (on a copy, so the cell can be re-run)
X_holdout = X_test.copy()
X_holdout["auth_method"] = X_holdout["auth_method"].map(auth_strength)
X_holdout["is_no_auth"] = (X_holdout["auth_method"] == 0)  # 0 = "No Authentication" after the mapping
X_holdout["has_cvv_retry"] = (X_holdout["cvv_retry_count"] > 0)
X_holdout = X_holdout.drop(columns="id")
y_holdout = y_test.astype(int)

print("Unmapped values:", X_holdout["auth_method"].isna().sum())  # should be 0
print("Same columns as X:", list(X_holdout.columns) == list(X.columns))

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

def evaluate(clf):
    pipe = Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("clf", clf)])
    res = cross_validate(pipe, X, y, cv=skf, scoring=["roc_auc", "average_precision"], n_jobs=-1)
    return {k: f"{v.mean():.4f} ± {v.std():.4f}" for k, v in res.items() if k.startswith("test_")}

models = {
    "logreg": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced"),
    "hgb": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=500, early_stopping=True, random_state=42),
    "lightgbm": LGBMClassifier(learning_rate=0.05, n_estimators=500, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42),
    "random_forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42),
    }

In [34]:
## Tune models to choose the best one for the final evaluation on the holdout set.
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import randint, uniform, loguniform

# 3 folds is enough with ~560k rows and halves the cost; the winner is re-checked with the 5-fold `skf` below.
tune_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

# Logistic Regression: few knobs and cheap fits, so an exhaustive grid covers the space.
logreg_search = GridSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))]),
    param_grid={
        "clf__C": np.logspace(-3, 2, 6),             # regularization strength
        "clf__class_weight": [None, "balanced"],     # AP is rank-based, so this mainly changes calibration
    },
    cv=tune_cv,
    scoring="average_precision",
    n_jobs=-1,
)
logreg_search.fit(X, y)

# LightGBM: many interacting continuous params, so random search samples them better than a grid.
# n_jobs=1 inside LightGBM because the search already runs folds in parallel (avoids oversubscription).
lgbm_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("clf", LGBMClassifier(subsample_freq=1, n_jobs=1, random_state=42, verbose=-1))]),
    param_distributions={
        "clf__num_leaves": randint(4, 40),             # push below 15
        "clf__min_child_samples": randint(150, 1000),  # push above 500
        "clf__subsample": uniform(0.2, 0.5),           # 0.2–0.7, push below 0.5
        "clf__colsample_bytree": uniform(0.5, 0.4),    # 0.5–0.9
        "clf__learning_rate": loguniform(0.01, 0.06),
        "clf__n_estimators": randint(500, 2500),       # lower lr needs more trees
    },
    n_iter=40,
    cv=tune_cv,
    scoring="average_precision",
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42,
)
lgbm_search.fit(X, y)

for name, search in [("logreg", logreg_search), ("lightgbm", lgbm_search)]:
    print(f"{name}: best CV PR-AUC = {search.best_score_:.4f}")
    print({k.removeprefix("clf__"): v for k, v in search.best_params_.items()}, "\n")

# Re-score the tuned models with the same 5-fold `skf` as the baselines, so the numbers are comparable.
models["logreg_tuned"] = logreg_search.best_estimator_.named_steps["clf"]
models["lightgbm_tuned"] = lgbm_search.best_estimator_.named_steps["clf"]
for name in ["logreg_tuned", "lightgbm_tuned"]:
    cv_results[name] = evaluate(models[name])
pd.DataFrame(cv_results).T

Hold-out test set¶

Fit on the whole training set, then score the 20% X_test we set aside at the start (never used during EDA or CV).

In [41]:
# Tuned LightGBM is the chosen model; tuned LogReg stays as the simpler reference.
best = "lightgbm_tuned"

fitted = {}
holdout_results = {}
for name in ["logreg_tuned", best]:
    fitted[name] = Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("clf", models[name])]).fit(X, y)
    proba = fitted[name].predict_proba(X_holdout)[:, 1]
    holdout_results[name] = {"roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_holdout, proba), "average_precision": average_precision_score(y_holdout, proba)}

pd.DataFrame(holdout_results).T.round(4)

Choosing a decision threshold¶

predict() uses 0.5 by default, which is a poor fit with 1.7% fraud. We pick thresholds from the out-of-fold predictions on the training set (picking them on the hold-out set would make its scores optimistic), and then check how they do on the hold-out set.

In [43]:
best_pipe = Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("clf", models[best])])
oof_proba = cross_val_predict(best_pipe, X, y, cv=skf, method="predict_proba", n_jobs=-1)[:, 1]
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y, oof_proba)
f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-12)

thresholds = {"default 0.5": 0.5, "max F1": thr[np.argmax(f1[:-1])]}
for target in [0.7, 0.8, 0.9]:
    thresholds[f"recall >= {target}"] = thr[np.where(rec[:-1] >= target)[0][-1]]

holdout_proba = fitted[best].predict_proba(X_holdout)[:, 1]
rows = {}
for rule, t in thresholds.items():
    pred = holdout_proba >= t
    tp = (pred & (y_holdout == 1)).sum()
    rows[rule] = {
        "threshold": t,
        "precision": tp / pred.sum(),
        "recall": tp / (y_holdout == 1).sum(),
        "pct_flagged": pred.mean(),
        "frauds_caught": tp,
        "false_alarms": (pred & (y_holdout == 0)).sum(),
    }
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

# Which features does the model rely on? (drop in PR-AUC when a column is shuffled)
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

sample = X_holdout.sample(30_000, random_state=42)
pi = permutation_importance(fitted[best], sample, y_holdout.loc[sample.index], scoring="average_precision", n_repeats=3, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=sample.columns).sort_values().plot(kind="barh", figsize=(8, 8), title="Permutation importance (drop in PR-AUC)")

Submission¶

The competition scores probabilities, not 0/1 labels, so the thresholds above are only for the business discussion and are not used here. We refit the chosen model on all labelled data (train + hold-out) and submit predict_proba for test.csv.

In [46]:
from sklearn.base import clone

# Refit on all labelled data (train + hold-out) so the final model sees every fraud.
# clone() so refitting doesn't change the already-fitted pipelines above.
X_full = pd.concat([X, X_holdout])
y_full = pd.concat([y, y_holdout])
final_model = Pipeline([("prep", clone(preprocess)), ("clf", clone(models[best]).set_params(n_jobs=-1))]).fit(X_full, y_full)

# Same feature engineering as the training and hold-out sets.
test = pd.read_csv("../data/raw/test.csv")
X_sub = test.drop(columns="id")
X_sub["auth_method"] = X_sub["auth_method"].map(auth_strength)
X_sub["is_no_auth"] = (X_sub["auth_method"] == 0)  # 0 = "No Authentication" after the mapping
X_sub["has_cvv_retry"] = (X_sub["cvv_retry_count"] > 0)
assert list(X_sub.columns) == list(X.columns)
print("Unmapped values:", X_sub["auth_method"].isna().sum())  # should be 0

submission = pd.DataFrame({"id": test["id"], "is_fraud": final_model.predict_proba(X_sub)[:, 1]})
submission.to_csv("../data/submission/submission.csv", index=False)
print(submission.shape)
submission["is_fraud"].describe()

Save the model¶

joblib/pickle can't save this pipeline: preprocess uses a lambda and the cyclic() closures. cloudpickle stores those functions by value, so the saved file loads without re-running this notebook (it still needs the same sklearn and lightgbm versions).

In [47]:
import json
import pickle
import cloudpickle
import sklearn
import lightgbm

model_dir = Path("../models")
model_path = model_dir / f"{best}.pkl"
model_path.write_bytes(cloudpickle.dumps(final_model))

# Metadata next to the model: what it is, how it scored, and which library versions can load it.
metadata = {
    "model": best,
    "trained_on_rows": len(X_full),
    "params": final_model.named_steps["clf"].get_params(),
    "cv_5fold": cv_results[best],
    "holdout": {k: float(v) for k, v in holdout_results[best].items()},
    "versions": {"sklearn": sklearn.__version__, "lightgbm": lightgbm.__version__},
}
(model_dir / f"{best}.json").write_text(json.dumps(metadata, indent=2, default=str))

# Round-trip check: the loaded model must give the same probabilities as the one in memory.
loaded = pickle.loads(model_path.read_bytes())
assert np.allclose(loaded.predict_proba(X_sub.head(1000))[:, 1], final_model.predict_proba(X_sub.head(1000))[:, 1])
print(f"Saved {model_path} ({model_path.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB)")
